questions.prompt: In the gas (Drude) model of conduction, a steady electric field is applied to a metal. What happens to the AVERAGE velocity of the electrons?
options: It grows linearly with time, \(\bar u = qEt/m\), as for a free particle
It settles at a constant drift velocity proportional to the field, \(\bar u = \mu E\), because collisions keep resetting the momentum
It stays zero, because collisions randomize every direction
It is proportional to \(E^2\), since the energy gained goes as \(E^2\)
questions.explanation:
Between collisions each electron gains momentum \(qEt\), but every collision randomizes its velocity. Averaged over many carriers, the random parts cancel and the field part gives \(M\bar u = qE\tau\), so \(\bar u = (q\tau/M)E = \mu E\) (reader Eq. 3.10–3.12).
The figure shows the sawtooth: velocity builds, then resets at each collision, so the average is constant. That proportionality of current to field is Ohm's law.

questions.prompt: Electrons in a silicon bar have mobility \(\mu_n = 1000\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\). The field is \(E = 100\ \mathrm{V/cm}\). What is the drift speed?
questions.explanation:
\[v_{dr} = \mu_n E = 1000 \times 100 = 10^5\ \mathrm{cm/s}\]
That is 1 km/s, still 100 times slower than the random thermal speed (about \(10^7\) cm/s), so the drift is a small bias on top of very fast random motion.

questions.prompt: Mobility is defined by \(v_{dr} = \mu E\). What are its usual units in device work?
options: \(\mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\)
\(\mathrm{cm/s}\)
\(\mathrm{V\cdot s/cm^2}\)
\(\mathrm{S/cm}\)
questions.explanation:
\[\mu = \frac{v}{E} = \frac{\mathrm{cm/s}}{\mathrm{V/cm}} = \frac{\mathrm{cm^2}}{\mathrm{V\cdot s}}\]
cm/s is a velocity, V·s/cm² is the inverse, and S/cm is conductivity, \(\sigma = qn\mu\).

questions.prompt: Electrons in silicon have an effective mass \(m^* = 0.26\,m_0\) (\(m_0 = 9.11\times10^{-31}\) kg) and a mean free time between collisions of \(\tau = 10^{-13}\) s. Using \(\mu = q\tau/m^*\), what is the mobility in \(\mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\)?
questions.explanation:
Work in SI units, then convert:
\[\mu = \frac{q\tau}{m^*} = \frac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{-13})}{0.26 \times 9.11\times10^{-31}} = 0.0676\ \mathrm{m^2/(V\cdot s)}\]
\[1\ \mathrm{m^2} = 10^4\ \mathrm{cm^2} \Rightarrow \mu \approx 676\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\]
That's the right order of magnitude for electrons in lightly doped silicon. Common mistake: forgetting the \(10^4\) conversion (answer 0.068).

questions.prompt: Copper has about \(8.5\times10^{22}\) free electrons per cm³ and an electron mobility of about \(43\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\). Using \(\sigma = qn\mu\), what is its resistivity in µΩ·cm?
questions.explanation:
\[\sigma = qn\mu = (1.602\times10^{-19})(8.5\times10^{22})(43) = 5.86\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{S/cm}\]
\[\rho = 1/\sigma = 1.71\times10^{-6}\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm} \approx 1.71\ \mu\Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\]
That matches the handbook value for copper (1.7 µΩ·cm). Its mobility is LOWER than silicon's; copper conducts well because \(n\) is enormous, not because \(\mu\) is large.

questions.prompt: An aluminium interconnect on a chip has resistivity \(\rho = 2.7\ \mu\Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\). It is 1 mm long, 1 µm wide and 0.5 µm thick. What is its resistance?
questions.explanation:
Convert everything to cm: \(L = 0.1\) cm, \(A = (10^{-4})(0.5\times10^{-4}) = 5\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{cm^2}\).
\[R = \rho\frac{L}{A} = 2.7\times10^{-6}\cdot\frac{0.1}{5\times10^{-9}} = 54\ \Omega\]
Tens of ohms is significant on a chip, which is why long wires need care. Common mistake: mixing µm and cm (off by factors of \(10^4\)).

questions.prompt: A copper wire with a 1 mm² cross-section carries 1 A. Copper has \(n = 8.5\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) free electrons. What is the electrons' average DRIFT speed in µm/s?
questions.explanation:
\(J = I/A = 1\ \mathrm{A} / 0.01\ \mathrm{cm^2} = 100\ \mathrm{A/cm^2}\), and \(J = qnv\):
\[v = \frac{J}{qn} = \frac{100}{(1.602\times10^{-19})(8.5\times10^{22})} = 7.34\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm/s} \approx 73.4\ \mu\mathrm{m/s}\]
Gotcha: the electrons crawl at less than 0.1 mm/s, while their random thermal speed is about \(10^{7}\) cm/s. The signal travels fast because the field, not the electrons, propagates down the wire. Common mistake: forgetting to convert mm² to cm² (\(1\ \mathrm{mm^2} = 0.01\ \mathrm{cm^2}\)).

questions.prompt: A field points in the \(+x\) direction in a conductor whose carriers are electrons, so the electrons drift toward \(-x\). In which direction does the current density \(J\) point?
options: \(-x\), the direction the electrons move
There is no net current, because the electrons' random velocities cancel
\(+x\) only if holes are also present
\(+x\), along the field: negative charge moving in \(-x\) is a current in \(+x\)
questions.explanation:
\(J = (-q)\,n\,v\) with \(v = -\mu_n E\) gives \(J = qn\mu_n E\), which is parallel to \(E\). The reader's sign bookkeeping (Eq. 3.14–3.15) shows positive and negative carriers both add to the conductivity: \(\sigma = q^2(N^+\tau^+/M^+ + N^-\tau^-/M^-)\).
Random thermal velocities do cancel; the drift velocity does not.

questions.prompt: Heating a metal wire raises its resistance (copper's conductivity drops about 30% from 273 K to 373 K). In the Drude picture, what causes this?
options: Heating frees fewer electrons, so n drops
Faster thermal motion makes the electrons drift backwards
Stronger lattice vibrations scatter electrons more often, shortening the mean free time τ and so lowering the mobility; the electron density barely changes
Heat ionizes impurities, which add electrons that block conduction
questions.explanation:
\(\sigma = nq^2\tau/m\). In a metal \(n\) is fixed (one electron per atom). Reader Sec. 3.2.7: electrons pass through a perfect periodic lattice unscattered; scattering comes from deviations from periodicity, namely thermal vibrations (phonons) and impurities.
More vibration means shorter \(\tau\), lower \(\mu\) and lower \(\sigma\). (In a semiconductor the opposite usually wins, because \(n\) rises exponentially with temperature.)

questions.prompt: Preview of silicon's carriers: the gas model allows positive AND negative carriers, \(\sigma = q(n\mu_n + p\mu_p)\). Pure silicon at 300 K has \(n = p = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(\mu_n = 1350\) and \(\mu_p = 480\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\). What is its resistivity in kΩ·cm?
questions.explanation:
\[\sigma = q\,n_i(\mu_n+\mu_p) = (1.602\times10^{-19})(10^{10})(1830) = 2.93\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{S/cm}\]
\[\rho = 1/\sigma \approx 3.41\times10^{5}\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm} = 341\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\]
That is about \(10^{11}\) times copper's resistivity. Upcoming skills explain why silicon has so few carriers and how adding dopants makes it useful.

questions.prompt: Preview of sheet resistance: a thin doped film has resistivity \(\rho = 10^{-3}\ \Omega\cdot\mathrm{cm}\) and thickness \(t = 0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). A resistor drawn in it is 10 times longer than it is wide (\(L/W = 10\)). What is its resistance?
questions.explanation:
\[R = \rho\frac{L}{W t} = \frac{\rho}{t}\cdot\frac{L}{W} = \frac{10^{-3}}{0.5\times10^{-4}} \times 10 = 20\ \Omega \times 10 = 200\ \Omega\]
The width cancels except through the ratio \(L/W\). The combination \(\rho/t\) (here 20 Ω) depends only on the film, so an IC designer just counts 'squares' of length/width. That quantity is the sheet resistance, coming up next.

questions.prompt: Preview of drift in silicon: electrons and holes have similar mean free times, but a hole's effective mass is larger than an electron's. With \(\mu = q\tau/m^*\), which carrier has the higher mobility, and what follows for transistors?
options: Holes, because heavier particles keep their momentum longer
Electrons; so for the same size and voltages, electron-based (n-type) devices conduct more current
They are equal, since mobility depends only on τ
Holes, because they are positive and are pushed along the field
questions.explanation:
\(\mu \propto 1/m^*\) at fixed \(\tau\), so lighter electrons are more mobile. The reader quotes typical silicon values of about \(\mu_n \approx 1000\) and \(\mu_p \approx 400\ \mathrm{cm^2/(V\cdot s)}\) ('electrons go faster as they are lighter').
Later you'll see that this is why an NMOS transistor carries more current than a PMOS of the same size. The sign of the charge decides the drift DIRECTION, not the speed.
